To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

plasminogen-binding by oral streptcoci was specific and lysin-dependent, that the bacteria were capable of activating plasminogen in the absence of exogenous plasminogen activation, that the streptococcus were capable of activating the plasminogen that was bound, but that the streptcoci were not capable of degrading fibrin in the absence of plasmin.
the oral streptococcus strains isolated from both dental plaque (healthy) and inflammatory lesions (diseased) were capable of binding plasmin, activating it, but not degrading the fibrin matrix.
the oral streptococcus strains isolated from plaque as well as from inflammatory lesions bound plasmin with approximately the same avidity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of plasmin binding by oral strepococci.
the characterization of a virulence factor that has been shown to be important in the pathogenesis of many different types of infections.
the role of plasmonogen in oral diseases and in particular, the role of plasmongen binding by oral strepococci in the pathogenesis of dental caries and periodontal diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the streptococi isolated from the supragingival plaques and inflammatory lesions are capable of binding plasminogens, and this binding is specific and lysine dependent.
plasminogen is bound by oral streptoccoci and that this binding may be of significance in relation to their pathogenicity.
plasminogen binds to a number of proteins in the cell wall and/or surface of oral streptoccoci.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the streptococcic binding to plasminogen is a common property among oral streptococcus and that the binding proteins are glycolytic enzymes.
the oral streptococcus strains from both plaque and inflammatory lesions bound plasmin with the same affinity and specificity.
the oral streptococcus strains from plaque and pus have a similar plasminogen-binding capacity, and that the binding proteins are mainly glycolytic enzymes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
plasminogen is a universal ligand for bacteria, and that it is not only a virulence factor for pathogenic bacteria, but also a virulence factor that may be utilized by commensal organisms.
plasminogen-binding is not unique to pathogenic streptococcal species.
plasminogen binds to a variety of bacterial species, both commensal and pathogenic, and that the binding is mediated by a number of proteins.
